title: Louis Vuitton Returns to a Looted Workshop at Asnières, 1871
dek: After the siege of Paris, a trunk-maker found his workshop stripped and his workers gone, and chose to start again at a new address.

story.event: Rebuilding the trunk business after the Asnières workshop was looted in the war of 1870-71
story.summary: During the Franco-Prussian War and the siege of Paris in 1870-71, Louis Vuitton's trunk workshop at Asnières was looted, his tools taken and his workers scattered, and orders stopped. Within months he opened a new shop at 1 rue Scribe in Paris, and in 1872 introduced a beige-and-red striped canvas in place of his grey one. The Asnières workshop was soon working again and is still in use.
paragraphs: In 1859 Louis Vuitton moved his trunk workshop out of Paris to Asnières, on the banks of the Seine, taking about twenty employees with him so that he could use the river for transport. He moved his family there too. He had opened his own business in 1854, and his flat-topped trunk, covered in grey canvas and easy to stack on trains and ships, had sold well. In 1867 he won a bronze medal at the Exposition Universelle in Paris.

The war with Prussia in 1870 stopped all of it. Paris was besieged, and Numéro, telling the house's history, says the workshops were looted and orders suspended. Biography.com gives the fullest account: when the siege ended on 28 January 1871, Vuitton, then 49, went back to Asnières and found the village in ruins, his staff dispersed, his equipment stolen and his workshop destroyed. None of these accounts records what he said or thought at the time. They record what he did.

He started again. Within months, by Biography.com's account, he had a shop at a new address, 1 rue Scribe, near the Opéra in the heart of the new Paris, on a street that was home to the Jockey Club. The trunks changed as well. In 1872 he brought out a design in beige canvas with red stripes instead of the plain grey, and Numéro ties the striped canvases and lighter colours directly to the rebuilding that followed the war.

The workshop by the river was working again within the decade. Students from the École Supérieure de Commerce de Paris visited it at least five times in the 1870s, 1880s and 1890s, according to the school's archives. Vuitton ran the house from rue Scribe for about twenty more years, until his death in February 1892, when his son Georges took over. Five generations of the family lived in the house beside the Asnières workshop, everything Louis Vuitton made came from there until 1977, and in 2017 about 200 people still worked in it.

quote.text: Perhaps its destruction has been brought about only that it may be raised up again to a better destiny. Oftentimes a reverse has but made room for more prosperous fortune. Many structures have fallen only to rise to a greater height.
quote.work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium)
quote.locator: Letter XCI, "On the Lesson to be Drawn from the Burning of Lyons", section 13
quote.source_title: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 91, tr. Richard M. Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, volume 2, 1920), Wikisource
quote.connection: Seneca, consoling a friend whose home city had burned in a single night, allowed that a ruin can make room for something better, and was careful to say perhaps. Vuitton's rebuilt house bears him out only in hindsight; in early 1871 there was a stripped workshop and a choice to begin again.

reflection: Vuitton did not put the old business back exactly as it had been. He moved the shop, changed the canvas and kept the workshop by the river. Rebuilding after a loss you did not cause is rarely a return to how things were. It is a run of small choices about what to keep and what to leave behind.

You may have something of your own that was interrupted this year: a plan, a habit, a piece of work knocked off course by events, by other people's decisions or simply by tiredness. You do not have to restore it as it was. Seneca's perhaps is honest. Some rebuilding turns out better and some only different, and you can begin without knowing which.
invitation: Choose one routine or piece of work that was interrupted and has not restarted. Write down one part worth keeping and one part you would not put back, and leave the rest for another day.

sources.title: Louis Vuitton (portrait, Maison de luxe)
sources.supports: Born 4 August 1821; own house founded 1854; flat trunk of 1858 covered in grey Trianon canvas; 1859 workshop at Asnières for space and river transport, still active; the war of 1870 interrupting his rise, the workshops looted and orders suspended; rebuilding almost at once and a new shop at 1 rue Scribe near the Opéra; striped canvases and lighter colours introduced with the rebuilding.

sources.title: Louis Vuitton (Vogue Spy biography)

research_notes: The documentary record of this episode is thin: no letter, interview or memoir by Louis Vuitton about 1870-71 was found, and every account is a later secondary history, so the story says plainly that none records what he thought and attributes the details. The extent of the damage differs between sources: Vogue and Bonjour Paris say the workshop was 'looted and destroyed'; Numéro says the workshops were pillaged and orders suspended; Biography.com says Asnières was in ruins, staff dispersed, equipment stolen and the shop destroyed; a FashionNetwork report on Caroline Bongrand's 2021 book (blocked for the verifier, so not cited) says Prussian forces set fire to the main atelier in 1870, burning most records of his personal life; a dealer's blog (now offline) put the damage during the Paris Commune of 1871 rather than the Prussian siege. Since the Asnières site still stands and was visited by ESCP students in the 1870s, the story says 'looted' and attributes 'destroyed' to Biography.com, and does not say who caused the damage. Striped canvas: Vogue and Biography.com date the beige-and-red stripe to 1872; the English Wikipedia company article, citing Martin's Contemporary Fashion (1995), gives 1876 for a beige-and-brown stripe, which appears to be a second, later striped canvas; the story uses 1872 for the red stripe only. Biography.com contrasts rue Scribe with Vuitton's 'previous location in Asnières', which confuses the Paris shop with the workshop; the story uses only its description of the street. Age 49 is computed from Numéro's birth date of 4 August 1821. The 1859 move of 'some twenty employees' is from ESCP's archive note. Seneca's letter consoles Aebutius Liberalis after the fire that destroyed Lugdunum (Lyon); Letter 91 is in volume 2 of Gummere's Loeb translation (1920), and the passage is section 13.
